subtopic_detail: Admission threshold for bronchiolitis in a well-perfused infant with borderline saturations and adequate feeding
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar at a tertiary emergency department. A 4 month old term infant is brought in during winter with 3 days of coryza and 1 day of cough. His mother reports he has been drinking about 60 percent of his usual feeds and had a normal wet nappy 2 hours ago. He has no apnoeas and has not required any admissions previously.

On examination he is alert with mild subcostal recession, respiratory rate 55 per minute, heart rate 148 per minute, temperature 37.4 degC and capillary refill 2 seconds. Auscultation reveals bilateral fine crackles and expiratory wheeze. His oxygen saturation on room air is 91 percent on repeat measurement over 5 minutes and rises to 94 percent transiently while alert. Nasopharyngeal aspirate is positive for RSV. He lives 15 minutes from the hospital with two well older siblings.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 148 /min, blood pressure 88/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 55 /min, SpO2 91% on room air, temperature 37.4 degC
data_table.Work of breathing: Mild subcostal recession, no head bob, no tracheal tug, no grunting
data_table.Feeding: Approximately 60% of usual intake over the last 12 hours, last wet nappy 2 hours ago
data_table.Clinical: Alert, well perfused, bilateral fine crackles and expiratory wheeze

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for inpatient observation with low flow nasal cannula oxygen titrated to maintain oxygen saturation at 92 percent or above with hourly feeding review
options.rationale: Persistent SpO2 below 92 percent on room air in a bronchiolitis infant meets AU admission criteria; feeding below 50 to 75 percent of normal is a further indication and low flow oxygen with feed review is standard ward care. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Give a single trial of nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg and admit only if the respiratory rate fails to fall by 20 percent within 30 minutes of the trial
options.rationale: Salbutamol trials are not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months and response is not a validated admission criterion in the AU pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg per kg daily for 3 days and reassess feeding after the first dose to guide the disposition decision
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids are not indicated in acute viral bronchiolitis under 12 months and do not alter disposition. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Discharge home on room air with a bronchiolitis parent information leaflet and arrange a general practitioner review the following morning within 12 to 18 hours
options.rationale: Discharge is not safe with SpO2 below 92 percent and reduced feeding under 75 percent; both are AU admission triggers regardless of proximity to hospital. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Start high flow humidified nasal cannula oxygen therapy at 2 L per kg per minute in the emergency department before making any admission or transfer decision
options.rationale: High flow is reserved for infants failing standard low flow oxygen or with moderate to severe work of breathing; escalation before a trial of low flow is not the AU first step. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months is managed with supportive care alone; bronchodilators, corticosteroids and antibiotics are not routinely indicated in the Australian guideline. Admission criteria in AU tertiary paediatric emergency departments include persistent room air SpO2 below 92 percent, feeding less than 50 to 75 percent of normal, moderate to severe work of breathing, apnoeas, dehydration, or clinician concern in a family without safe follow up. Low flow nasal cannula oxygen (up to 2 L per minute) is the first line respiratory support; high flow is reserved for those failing low flow, and continuous positive airway pressure or transfer to a paediatric intensive care unit is considered next. Feeding is often the earliest and most sensitive marker of severity.
key_points: AU admission triggers: SpO2 below 92% persistently, feeds less than 50 to 75% of normal, moderate to severe work of breathing.
Low flow nasal cannula oxygen is the first line respiratory support before high flow.
Bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics are not routinely indicated in bronchiolitis under 12 months.
explanation.pearls: Feeding under 50 to 75 percent of normal intake in a bronchiolitis infant is an admission trigger in its own right in the AU pathway even if the SpO2 is 92 percent or above.

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic versus observation decision in uncomplicated acute otitis media in a well 18 month old with bilateral disease
stem:
You are a general practitioner reviewing an 18 month old girl brought in by her father with 2 days of ear tugging, low grade fever and disturbed sleep. She is otherwise well, immunisations are up to date and she has had one previous episode of acute otitis media 6 months ago that resolved with observation alone. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander and lives in an urban home with two well parents.

On examination she is alert and playful, temperature 38.1 degC, and both tympanic membranes are bulging, opaque and immobile on pneumatic otoscopy. There is no discharge, no mastoid tenderness and no meningism. Feeding is 80 percent of normal and she has had five wet nappies in the last 24 hours. There are no red flags for complications and her father is comfortable returning if things worsen.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 128 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.1 degC
data_table.ENT: Both tympanic membranes bulging, opaque, immobile on pneumatic otoscopy; no discharge or mastoid tenderness
data_table.Systemic: Alert, playful, feeding 80% normal, five wet nappies in 24 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe oral cefuroxime 15 mg per kg twice daily for 5 days now with paracetamol and ibuprofen for symptom control and review in 72 hours
options.rationale: Cephalosporins are not first line for uncomplicated acute otitis media in AU and add resistance risk without benefit over amoxicillin. (Source: eTG: Acute Otitis Media)

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin 30 mg per kg twice daily for 5 days now given bilateral acute otitis media with fever under 2 years plus regular analgesia and safety net advice
options.rationale: Bilateral acute otitis media in a child under 2 years or with fever above 38 degC is a specific AU indication for immediate amoxicillin rather than a delayed script or observation. (Source: eTG: Acute Otitis Media)

options.text: Observe with regular analgesia and provide a delayed prescription for oral amoxicillin to be filled only if symptoms have not improved after 48 hours of watchful waiting at home
options.rationale: Delayed prescription is offered for unilateral acute otitis media without fever in a well older child; bilateral disease under 2 years with fever needs immediate treatment. (Source: eTG: Acute Otitis Media)

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid 22.5 mg per kg twice daily for 7 days now due to recurrent acute otitis media with a second episode within 12 months
options.rationale: Amoxicillin plus clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure after 48 to 72 hours of amoxicillin, not first line for a second episode months apart. (Source: eTG: Acute Otitis Media)

options.text: Refer to an ear nose and throat specialist today for consideration of tympanocentesis with culture directed antibiotic choice before starting any empirical oral antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Tympanocentesis is reserved for treatment failure, immunocompromise or suppurative complications; it is not needed in an uncomplicated first presentation. (Source: eTG: Acute Otitis Media)

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media in Australian non-Aboriginal children under 2 years with bilateral disease or associated fever above 38 degC is a specific indication for immediate amoxicillin rather than observation with a delayed script. Unilateral disease in an older well child without fever can be managed with analgesia and a delayed prescription filled at 48 hours if symptoms persist. Amoxicillin 30 mg per kg twice daily for 5 days is first line; amoxicillin plus clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure at 48 to 72 hours. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children have a lower threshold for immediate antibiotics and longer courses because of higher rates of chronic suppurative otitis media.
key_points: Bilateral acute otitis media under 2 years or fever above 38 degC: immediate amoxicillin.
Unilateral acute otitis media in a well child over 2 years: delayed script at 48 hours is reasonable.
Amoxicillin plus clavulanate is second line for treatment failure at 48 to 72 hours, not first line.
explanation.pearls: Immediate amoxicillin 30 mg per kg twice daily for 5 days is the AU first line for any child with bilateral acute otitis media under 2 years, not the delayed script offered in older well children.

subtopic_detail: Combined oral contraceptive request in a Gillick competent 15 year old without parental involvement
stem:
You are a general practitioner in Victoria seeing a 15 year old girl who requests the combined oral contraceptive pill. She attends alone and has not told her parents she is sexually active with one male partner of 15 years old. Menarche was at 12 years and cycles are regular. She has no migraine, no venous thromboembolism, no personal or family history of breast cancer and does not smoke. Blood pressure is 112/68 mmHg and body mass index is 22 kg per m2.

She understands why the pill works and is asked to explain how she would take it, what she would do about a missed pill and where she would seek help if she had chest pain or a swollen leg. Her answers are clear and appropriate. She declines to involve either parent, states her home is stable and safe, and there is no coercion or exploitation on your assessment. She agrees to a return visit in 3 months and to a chlamydia and gonorrhoea nucleic acid amplification test today.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, body mass index 22 kg/m2
data_table.Sexual health: One male partner age 15, condom use inconsistent, no dyspareunia or bleeding
data_table.Medical: No migraine, no venous thromboembolism, no breast cancer family history, non smoker
data_table.Assessment: Gillick competent on questioning; declines parental involvement; no safeguarding red flags

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Decline to prescribe until at least one parent attends a review appointment to provide consent for hormonal contraception because she is under the age of 16 years today
options.rationale: Australian law recognises Gillick competence for consent to health care in minors; a 15 year old assessed competent may consent without parental involvement. (Source: RACGP: Adolescent Contraception)

options.text: Prescribe the combined oral contraceptive pill and inform her parents by telephone once the script is dispensed because minors under 16 years cannot maintain confidentiality of prescribing
options.rationale: Breaching confidentiality without her consent is not lawful and undermines therapeutic engagement; disclosure is only mandated for a mandatory reporting risk. (Source: RACGP: Adolescent Contraception)

options.text: Prescribe the combined oral contraceptive pill and offer a discussion of long acting reversible contraception options as she is Gillick competent with no medical contraindications
options.rationale: She meets Gillick competence with no contraindications; AU guidance actively promotes discussion of long acting reversible contraception alongside prescribing the requested method. (Source: RACGP: Adolescent Contraception)

options.text: Refuse the combined oral contraceptive pill and instead offer condoms alone until she turns 16 years because barrier methods do not require prescription and avoid confidentiality issues
options.rationale: Condoms alone give inferior pregnancy protection and denying hormonal contraception to a competent adolescent is neither guideline concordant nor legally required. (Source: RACGP: Adolescent Contraception)

options.text: Report the sexual activity to child protection services under mandatory reporting laws before deciding whether to issue any contraceptive prescription to this patient today
options.rationale: Consensual sexual activity between similarly aged 15 year olds without exploitation is not a mandatory report in Victoria; a report here would breach confidentiality without cause. (Source: Victorian Child Wellbeing and Safety Framework)
source_refs: Victorian Child Wellbeing and Safety Framework

explanation.summary: Australian law and Royal Australian College of General Practitioners guidance recognise Gillick competence for adolescents consenting to health care. A minor under 16 years assessed as understanding the nature, purpose and consequences of a treatment may consent without parental involvement. Mandatory reporting is triggered by exploitation, coercion, a significant age gap or a partner in a position of power, not by consensual activity between similarly aged 15 year olds. Long acting reversible contraception is the most effective option and should be offered at the same visit even when a specific method is requested. Confidentiality is central to adolescent engagement; disclosure without consent is only justified for a safeguarding risk.
key_points: Gillick competence allows minors under 16 to consent to their own health care in Australia.
Consensual sexual activity between similarly aged 15 year olds is not automatically a mandatory report.
Offer long acting reversible contraception at the same visit even when a specific method is requested.
explanation.pearls: A Gillick competent 15 year old with no contraindications may be prescribed combined oral contraception confidentially in Australia; mandatory reporting only follows exploitation or a significant age gap, not similarly aged consensual sex.

sources.label: Victorian Child Wellbeing and Safety Framework

subtopic_detail: Follow up plan for a 40 hour old term breastfed newborn with a serum bilirubin just below the phototherapy line on the AU nomogram
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 40 hour old term breastfed girl on the postnatal ward. She was born at 39 plus 2 weeks by normal vaginal delivery, weighed 3.35 kg and has lost 5 percent of her birth weight. Feeding is established, latching well every 2 to 3 hours and there are five heavy wet nappies in the last 24 hours. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, has no cephalhaematoma and no family history of haemolytic disease.

Her mother is blood group O RhD positive with no red cell antibodies. The baby is A RhD positive with a negative direct antiglobulin test. Transcutaneous bilirubin measurement is 235 micromol/L confirmed by a serum total bilirubin of 240 micromol/L. On the Australian consensus phototherapy nomogram for a 40 hour old at 38 plus weeks with no risk factors the threshold line sits at 280 micromol/L. She is alert, well perfused, has normal tone and no scleral icterus below the nipple line.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 138 /min, respiratory rate 42 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Investigations: Serum total bilirubin 240 micromol/L (phototherapy line 280 at this age), direct antiglobulin test negative, group A RhD positive
data_table.Feeding: Breastfeeding every 2 to 3 hours, five wet nappies in 24 hours, 5% weight loss from birth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intensive multiple phototherapy immediately in a special care nursery cot with continuous exchange transfusion preparation before repeating any measurement in the next few hours
options.rationale: Her serum bilirubin sits below the phototherapy line and there is no evidence of severe or rapidly rising haemolytic jaundice to warrant intensive phototherapy or exchange preparation. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Give a single top up feed of infant formula 60 mL now and continue routine postnatal observations without any repeat bilirubin measurement or additional feeding assessment planned in the next 24 hours
options.rationale: Formula top ups are not first line in a well established breastfed baby with normal weight loss and normal urine output; repeat bilirubin remains needed to check trajectory. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Discharge home with the community midwife the same day and arrange a general practitioner review at 2 weeks of age for the routine newborn assessment without any earlier repeat measurement
options.rationale: A bilirubin within 40 to 50 micromol/L of the phototherapy line at under 48 hours needs repeat measurement in 12 to 24 hours; discharge without follow up risks missing a crossing trajectory. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Continue breastfeeding with lactation support, repeat serum bilirubin in 12 to 24 hours and plot against the age matched Australian phototherapy nomogram to track the trajectory over time
options.rationale: AU practice for a bilirubin within about 50 micromol/L of the line under 48 hours is to continue feeding, support breastfeeding and repeat in 12 to 24 hours to track the trajectory. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Request a full septic screen including blood culture and lumbar puncture and start intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin empirically while awaiting the results of the infection workup
options.rationale: There are no clinical features of sepsis in this well feeding afebrile baby; a septic screen and empiric antibiotics are not indicated for isolated jaundice within the safe zone. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice in the first week is common; the Australian consensus phototherapy nomogram plots total serum bilirubin against age in hours and gestation. Values below the phototherapy line but within about 50 micromol/L of it, especially in the first 48 hours, warrant repeat measurement in 12 to 24 hours because bilirubin can continue to rise. Direct antiglobulin negativity and maternal group compatibility make isolated ABO or rhesus haemolytic disease unlikely, but ongoing tracking is still required until levels plateau. Breastfeeding support, adequate hydration and follow up review are the mainstays; formula top ups are not first line in a well feeding baby with normal weight loss and urine output. Early discharge without a repeat bilirubin risks missing a crossing trajectory.
key_points: Values within about 50 micromol/L of the phototherapy line under 48 hours need repeat measurement in 12 to 24 hours.
The AU consensus nomogram is plotted by age in hours and gestation.
Support breastfeeding; formula top ups are not first line in a well feeding baby with normal weight loss.
explanation.pearls: A term breastfed newborn with a bilirubin within 50 micromol/L of the AU phototherapy line under 48 hours needs a repeat serum bilirubin in 12 to 24 hours to plot the trajectory, not immediate phototherapy or discharge.

reference_ranges.range: phototherapy line ~280 micromol/L at 40 hours (AU consensus nomogram)

subtopic_detail: Approach to a 3 year old with 6 days of fever and only 2 clinical criteria but supportive laboratory features suggestive of incomplete Kawasaki disease
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 3 year old boy admitted with 6 days of high spiking fevers to 39.6 degC that have not responded to paracetamol and ibuprofen. He is irritable and off his food but drinking fluids. He has bilateral non exudative conjunctival injection and a peeling red perineal rash but no cervical adenopathy, no lip changes and no extremity oedema. Two prior general practitioner visits considered viral infection.

A respiratory virus panel is negative, urinalysis shows sterile pyuria on microscopy and blood cultures at 48 hours are negative. Inflammatory markers show C reactive protein 128 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 82 mm/hr, platelet count 512 x10^9/L (elevated for age), white cell count 15.6 x10^9/L with neutrophil predominance, albumin 28 g/L (35 to 50) and alanine aminotransferase 68 U/L (5 to 45). Sodium is 132 mmol/L. An echocardiogram is available today.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 148 /min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 39.4 degC
data_table.Clinical: 6 days fever, bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, perineal desquamation; no lymphadenopathy or oral changes
data_table.Bloods: CRP 128 mg/L, ESR 82 mm/hr, platelets 512 x10^9/L, WCC 15.6, albumin 28 g/L, ALT 68 U/L, sodium 132 mmol/L
data_table.Investigations: Sterile pyuria on urinalysis; respiratory virus panel negative; blood cultures negative at 48 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue supportive care with regular paracetamol and observation for further clinical criteria to appear before committing to any specific inflammatory disease treatment during this admission today
options.rationale: Waiting for the classical 5 criteria misses the treatment window; supportive laboratory features with 2 criteria and fever above 5 days meet AU incomplete Kawasaki pathway thresholds. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Start intravenous flucloxacillin plus benzylpenicillin empirically for suspected occult bacterial infection while awaiting further culture results and additional infection screening tests today
options.rationale: Cultures are negative, viral panel negative and the picture (perineal desquamation, sterile pyuria, hepatitis, hyponatraemia, thrombocytosis) fits incomplete Kawasaki rather than a bacterial focus. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Give a stat dose of intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg per kg pulse without intravenous immunoglobulin and reassess response by day 8 of fever to guide ongoing management decisions
options.rationale: Intravenous immunoglobulin is first line in Kawasaki disease and should not be replaced by pulse steroid alone; steroid is added to high risk patients or given as rescue. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Arrange outpatient rheumatology review in 1 week to consider systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis before any inpatient anti inflammatory therapy is commenced during this current admission
options.rationale: Delaying decision by a week risks coronary artery aneurysm; the syndrome fits incomplete Kawasaki now and IVIG is time critical within 10 days of fever onset. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Give intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kg over 10 to 12 hours plus oral aspirin 3 to 5 mg per kg daily and arrange a baseline echocardiogram to look for coronary artery abnormalities
options.rationale: Fever 5 or more days with 2 clinical criteria plus supportive labs (CRP above 30, ESR above 40, plus 3 or more of albumin low, anaemia, ALT elevated, platelets high, WCC high, sterile pyuria) meets AU incomplete Kawasaki criteria for IVIG and low dose aspirin with baseline echocardiography. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease should be considered in any child with 5 or more days of fever and 2 or 3 principal clinical criteria plus supporting laboratory features because 15 to 20 percent of cases present incompletely. Supporting labs include C reactive protein above 30 mg/L or erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 40 mm/hr, and 3 or more of hypoalbuminaemia, anaemia, elevated alanine aminotransferase, thrombocytosis after day 7, leucocytosis and sterile pyuria. Baseline echocardiography looks for coronary artery abnormalities, but treatment should not wait for it if the diagnosis is otherwise clear. Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kg over 10 to 12 hours plus oral aspirin (3 to 5 mg per kg daily until markers normalise and echocardiography is clear at 6 to 8 weeks) is first line. High risk patients may receive adjunctive corticosteroid.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki: 5 or more days of fever, 2 to 3 clinical criteria plus supportive laboratory features.
Supportive labs: CRP above 30, ESR above 40, plus 3 or more of low albumin, anaemia, ALT high, platelets high, WCC high, sterile pyuria.
First line: intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kg plus low dose aspirin with baseline echocardiography.
explanation.pearls: Perineal desquamation and sterile pyuria are two supportive features that often clinch an incomplete Kawasaki diagnosis when the mucocutaneous criteria are incomplete; treat within 10 days of fever onset to reduce coronary artery aneurysm risk.

subtopic_detail: Nephrology referral criteria in a child with new IgA vasculitis and unexpected proteinuria on urinalysis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6 year old boy referred by his general practitioner with a palpable purpuric rash over his buttocks and lower legs for 5 days, migratory ankle pain and one episode of loose stool. He was well before the rash appeared 10 days after an upper respiratory illness. He has no headache, no oedema and no macroscopic haematuria; he has passed urine normally and there is no abdominal tenderness.

Examination shows blood pressure 108/68 mmHg (95th centile for age and height 108/68 mmHg), heart rate 96 per minute and no scrotal or facial swelling. Urinalysis is 3+ protein and 2+ blood on dipstick with red cell casts on microscopy. Spot urine protein to creatinine ratio is 320 mg per mmol (normal below 20). Serum creatinine is 42 micromol/L (25 to 60), estimated glomerular filtration rate is 92 mL per min per 1.73 m2 and albumin is 34 g/L. Coagulation and platelets are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 96 /min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Clinical: Palpable purpura buttocks and lower legs, migratory ankle pain, one loose stool; no oedema, no macroscopic haematuria
data_table.Urine: Dipstick 3+ protein, 2+ blood; red cell casts on microscopy; spot protein:creatinine ratio 320 mg/mmol (normal below 20)
data_table.Bloods: Creatinine 42 micromol/L, eGFR 92 mL/min/1.73m2, albumin 34 g/L, platelets normal, coagulation normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Refer urgently to a paediatric nephrologist today because nephrotic range proteinuria complicating IgA vasculitis meets AU criteria for early specialist review and biopsy consideration
options.rationale: Protein:creatinine ratio above 250 mg/mmol (nephrotic range) or persistent above 100 for 4 or more weeks in IgA vasculitis is an AU trigger for urgent nephrology referral and biopsy consideration. (Source: KHA-CARI: Paediatric Nephrotic Range Proteinuria)

options.text: Prescribe oral prednisolone 1 mg per kg daily for 2 weeks starting today to prevent renal involvement in this child with established IgA vasculitis and joint symptoms plus a purpuric rash
options.rationale: Corticosteroids reduce arthralgia and abdominal pain but do not prevent renal disease; commencing empirically without nephrology input in nephrotic range proteinuria is not first line. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein Purpura)

options.text: Reassure the family and arrange general practitioner review with a repeat urinalysis in 4 weeks then again in 3 months to monitor for evolving renal involvement in this benign self limiting condition
options.rationale: Nephrotic range proteinuria with red cell casts is not benign and needs urgent specialist review; the standard weekly then monthly surveillance schedule assumes normal or trace urine findings. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein Purpura)

options.text: Commence oral ramipril 2.5 mg once daily and salt restriction now to reduce proteinuria and defer any specialist input until 6 weeks of angiotensin blockade has demonstrated a clinical response
options.rationale: Angiotensin blockade is not first line in acute paediatric nephrotic range proteinuria without a diagnosis; nephrology guides use and biopsy comes first. (Source: KHA-CARI: Paediatric Nephrotic Range Proteinuria)

options.text: Give a single intravenous methylprednisolone pulse 30 mg per kg in the emergency department and discharge home to continue on daily oral prednisolone at general practitioner review only
options.rationale: Pulse steroid is a nephrology decision after biopsy in crescentic disease; discharge without nephrology input for nephrotic range proteinuria is unsafe. (Source: KHA-CARI: Paediatric Nephrotic Range Proteinuria)

explanation.summary: IgA vasculitis (formerly Henoch-Schoenlein purpura) is the commonest paediatric small vessel vasculitis and usually self limits. Renal involvement affects around a third of children in the first 6 months and is the main determinant of long term prognosis. All children with IgA vasculitis should have weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for the first month, fortnightly for 2 months, then monthly to 6 months. Persistent proteinuria above 100 mg per mmol for 4 or more weeks or any nephrotic range proteinuria (above 250 mg per mmol) triggers urgent nephrology referral and consideration of renal biopsy. Corticosteroids reduce joint and abdominal symptoms but do not prevent nephritis.
key_points: All IgA vasculitis children need urinalysis and blood pressure surveillance for at least 6 months.
Protein:creatinine ratio above 250 mg/mmol or persistent above 100 for 4 weeks triggers urgent nephrology referral.
Corticosteroids do not prevent nephritis; they reduce joint and abdominal symptoms only.
explanation.pearls: Nephrotic range proteinuria (protein:creatinine ratio above 250 mg/mmol) with red cell casts in new IgA vasculitis is an AU trigger for urgent paediatric nephrology referral, not for empirical prednisolone alone.

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic pathway in a stable 22 month old with witnessed aspiration event and normal early chest radiograph
stem:
You are the paediatric emergency registrar reviewing a 22 month old boy who choked while eating peanuts at his older brothers birthday 4 hours ago. He coughed forcefully, went red in the face for a few seconds and then settled. His parents describe intermittent coughing since but he has not been distressed and he is now playing on his mothers lap. He has no known respiratory disease and was previously well.

On examination he is alert and interactive, respiratory rate 26 per minute, heart rate 108 per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and temperature 36.9 degC. There is a mild expiratory wheeze audible over the right lower zone but air entry appears bilateral and there is no tracheal deviation. A supine inspiratory chest radiograph performed 20 minutes ago is reported as normal with no radiopaque foreign body, no lobar collapse and no obvious hyperinflation on the visualised lung fields.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 108 /min, blood pressure 96/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Clinical: Alert and interactive, mild expiratory wheeze over right lower zone, bilateral air entry, no tracheal deviation
data_table.Imaging: Supine inspiratory chest radiograph normal; no radiopaque foreign body, no lobar collapse, no obvious hyperinflation
data_table.History: Witnessed choking on peanuts 4 hours ago, transient distress then settled, intermittent cough since

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with parental advice to return if cough or breathing worsens because the child has a normal oxygen saturation and a chest radiograph reported as normal at the present time
options.rationale: A witnessed peanut aspiration with a focal wheeze is a strong clinical indication for bronchoscopy regardless of a normal saturation and an initially normal radiograph; early chest films are normal in around 20 percent. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

options.text: Refer urgently for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia today because history plus focal auscultatory findings meets the AU threshold for bronchoscopy regardless of the chest radiograph findings
options.rationale: A history of witnessed choking with any of persistent cough, focal wheeze or asymmetric air entry meets AU indications for rigid bronchoscopy even with a normal radiograph. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

options.text: Perform expiratory and lateral decubitus chest radiographs first and only proceed to bronchoscopy if there is unequivocal air trapping visible on the expiratory or decubitus film series
options.rationale: Expiratory or decubitus views can support the diagnosis but a normal series does not exclude foreign body; clinical history plus focal signs still mandates bronchoscopy. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

options.text: Start nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg and oral prednisolone 1 mg per kg for suspected viral wheeze and observe response over 2 hours before making any further airway intervention decision
options.rationale: A witnessed choke and focal wheeze is not viral wheeze; bronchodilators and steroids risk masking the picture and delay definitive bronchoscopy. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

options.text: Request a computed tomography scan of the chest with contrast today and decide on bronchoscopy based on the imaging findings after the paediatric radiologist has reviewed the study
options.rationale: Radiation is not first line when the pretest probability is high; bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic and does not need to await computed tomography. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

explanation.summary: Paediatric foreign body aspiration classically presents in a toddler with a witnessed choking episode followed by cough, wheeze or stridor. Peanuts, seeds and small toys are the commonest culprits. A normal supine inspiratory chest radiograph does not exclude the diagnosis; 20 percent of early films are normal. Expiratory films or lateral decubitus views may show unilateral air trapping. When history plus any of persistent cough, focal wheeze or asymmetric air entry are present, rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia is both diagnostic and therapeutic and should not wait for advanced imaging. Delayed diagnosis risks obstructive pneumonia, atelectasis and bronchiectasis.
key_points: Witnessed choking with persistent cough, focal wheeze or asymmetric air entry mandates rigid bronchoscopy.
A normal initial chest radiograph does not exclude foreign body aspiration.
Rigid bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic and comes before computed tomography.
explanation.pearls: In a toddler with a witnessed choke and a focal wheeze, rigid bronchoscopy is indicated even with a normal chest radiograph; up to 20 percent of early films are read normal in confirmed foreign body aspiration.

subtopic_detail: Recognition and initial stabilisation of critical coarctation of the aorta presenting as circulatory collapse in a 3 week old missed at the neonatal check
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a regional emergency department when parents bring in a 3 week old term boy with 24 hours of poor feeding, greyness during feeds and a mottled appearance. Birth weight was 3.4 kg and the newborn examination at 24 hours was reported as normal including pre and post ductal saturations of 96 percent. He passed the state hearing screen. There is no family history of congenital heart disease.

On arrival he is pale and mottled, capillary refill 4 seconds, cool peripheries, drowsy but rousable. Right brachial blood pressure is 96/58 mmHg while the right lower limb blood pressure is 58/34 mmHg. Right radial pulses are readily palpable, femoral pulses are weak and delayed on both sides. Auscultation reveals a soft ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge with a loud second heart sound. The liver is 3 cm below the costal margin. Pre ductal (right hand) saturation is 96 percent on room air; post ductal (right foot) saturation is 89 percent on room air. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.18, base excess minus 12, lactate 7.4 mmol/L, glucose 3.8 mmol/L. The nearest paediatric cardiac centre is 3 hours away by neonatal retrieval team.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 178 /min, respiratory rate 62 /min, temperature 36.4 degC
data_table.Perfusion: Right brachial BP 96/58 mmHg, right lower limb BP 58/34 mmHg, capillary refill 4 s, cool peripheries
data_table.Saturations: Pre-ductal (right hand) 96%, post-ductal (right foot) 89% on room air
data_table.Blood gas: pH 7.18, base excess -12, lactate 7.4 mmol/L, glucose 3.8 mmol/L
data_table.Cardiac: Soft left sternal edge ejection systolic murmur, loud second heart sound, liver 3 cm below costal margin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Give 20 mL per kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus intravenously immediately and reassess perfusion and lactate after the fluid bolus is complete without any additional therapy pending retrieval team arrival
options.rationale: Aggressive fluid boluses can precipitate pulmonary oedema in duct dependent systemic circulation; small measured boluses (5 to 10 mL per kg) with reassessment are preferred and prostaglandin is the priority. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease

options.text: Intubate immediately and commence intravenous adrenaline infusion at 0.1 mcg per kg per minute for cardiogenic shock support while awaiting the retrieval team for definitive transfer to the tertiary centre
options.rationale: Intubation may drop the arterial CO2 and worsen the left to right shunt and pulmonary steal; ventilation targets must protect ductal flow; inotrope alone without prostaglandin is not first line. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease

options.text: Start intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion at 10 nanograms per kg per minute now, contact the paediatric cardiac retrieval service and monitor for apnoea and hypotension during the infusion
options.rationale: Prostaglandin E1 at 5 to 20 nanograms per kg per minute reopens the arterial duct and restores lower body perfusion in duct dependent systemic circulation; apnoea and hypotension are the two main early adverse effects. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease

options.text: Commence oral propranolol 0.5 mg per kg for suspected hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy while awaiting the retrieval team and defer any additional intravenous therapy until the child arrives at the tertiary centre
options.rationale: The picture is upper to lower limb pressure gradient with weak femorals and post ductal desaturation, not hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy; beta blockade will worsen shock. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease

options.text: Provide face mask oxygen at 10 L per minute continuously to achieve pre ductal saturation of 100 percent before making any further therapeutic or transfer decision for this patient today
options.rationale: High inspired oxygen closes the arterial duct and worsens duct dependent systemic perfusion; target saturations are 75 to 85 percent in single ventricle physiology and around 85 to 92 percent in coarctation while duct is preserved. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease

explanation.summary: Critical coarctation of the aorta presents in the first weeks of life with shock as the arterial duct closes and lower body perfusion collapses. An upper to lower limb blood pressure gradient of 20 mmHg or greater, weak or absent femoral pulses and a pre to post ductal saturation gradient (arm minus foot) of 3 percent or more are the pathognomonic triad. Initial management is intravenous prostaglandin E1 5 to 20 nanograms per kg per minute to reopen the duct, cautious fluid resuscitation (5 to 10 mL per kg boluses reassessed), preservation of spontaneous ventilation and avoidance of high inspired oxygen which closes the duct and worsens the left to right pulmonary steal. Complications of prostaglandin include apnoea, fever, flushing and hypotension; be ready to intubate. Definitive treatment is surgical or catheter based repair after transfer to a paediatric cardiac centre.
key_points: Pre to post ductal saturation gradient of 3% or more (upper minus lower) is pathognomonic for duct dependent systemic obstruction.
Prostaglandin E1 5 to 20 nanograms per kg per minute reopens the arterial duct and restores lower body perfusion.
Avoid high FiO2 (closes duct) and large fluid boluses (worsens pulmonary oedema in duct dependent systemic circulation).
explanation.pearls: In a shocked neonate with a pre to post ductal saturation gap and weak femorals, start prostaglandin E1 at 10 nanograms per kg per minute before any large fluid bolus or high FiO2 and prepare for apnoea within 60 minutes of commencement.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease
RCH CPG: Duct Dependent Congenital Heart Disease

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis loading and maintenance in a woman with severe pre-eclampsia at 34 plus 3 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar at a metropolitan tertiary hospital reviewing a 32 year old primigravid woman at 34 plus 3 weeks with severe pre-eclampsia. She reports headache and epigastric pain today. Her booking blood pressure was 118/72 mmHg and today it is 168/112 mmHg on repeat measurement 15 minutes apart. Urine dipstick shows 3+ protein and spot protein to creatinine ratio is 92 mg per mmol.

Other bloods show platelets 118 x10^9/L (150 to 400), creatinine 92 micromol/L (baseline 62), alanine aminotransferase 88 U/L (5 to 45) and urate 0.41 mmol/L. Reflexes are brisk with 3 beats of ankle clonus. Cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 145 with normal variability, accelerations present and no decelerations. She has no known allergies. Intravenous labetalol has been commenced for blood pressure control and antenatal corticosteroid course is being organised. There is no known contraindication to magnesium sulfate and creatinine clearance is preserved.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 96 /min, blood pressure 168/112 mmHg on repeat, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Bloods: Platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 92 micromol/L (baseline 62), ALT 88 U/L (5-45), urate 0.41 mmol/L
data_table.Neurological: Headache, epigastric pain, brisk reflexes with 3 beats of ankle clonus
data_table.Foetal: Cardiotocograph baseline 145 /min, normal variability, accelerations present, no decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate magnesium sulfate regimen?

options.text: Give intramuscular magnesium sulfate 5 g into each buttock as a total loading dose of 10 g and repeat 5 g every 4 hours without any intravenous maintenance infusion pending delivery of the baby
options.rationale: Intramuscular Pritchard regimen is a resource limited fallback; the AU intravenous regimen (4 g load then 1 g/h) is preferred where infusion pumps and monitoring are available. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Withhold magnesium sulfate and use intravenous diazepam 10 mg bolus at seizure onset only because prophylactic magnesium sulfate is not evidence based in severe pre-eclampsia without an antecedent eclamptic seizure
options.rationale: Magpie trial evidence supports prophylactic magnesium sulfate in severe pre-eclampsia; benzodiazepines are second line at seizure. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Load with intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 5 minutes and follow with a maintenance intravenous infusion at 2 g per hour targeting therapeutic serum magnesium of 3.0 to 4.0 mmol/L
options.rationale: The AU loading dose is 4 g over 20 minutes with 1 g per hour maintenance; therapeutic monitoring is by clinical signs (reflexes, respiratory rate, urine output) rather than routine magnesium levels. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Load with intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g over 20 minutes and follow with a maintenance intravenous infusion at 1 g per hour for at least 24 hours after delivery with clinical monitoring
options.rationale: The RANZCOG AU regimen for severe pre-eclampsia seizure prophylaxis is 4 g load over 20 minutes then 1 g per hour for 24 hours after delivery, monitored by reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate 6 g bolus and titrate maintenance infusion between 2 g and 3 g per hour to serum magnesium level with the primary purpose of lowering the maternal blood pressure
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is a seizure prophylactic, not an antihypertensive; blood pressure is treated separately with labetalol, nifedipine or hydralazine. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia meets criteria when hypertension (blood pressure at least 160/110 mmHg) is accompanied by any severe feature such as symptoms (headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain), thrombocytopenia below 100 x10^9/L, transaminase above twice the upper limit of normal, creatinine rising above baseline, pulmonary oedema or foetal compromise. Prophylactic magnesium sulfate reduces the risk of eclampsia by around 60 percent based on the Magpie trial. The Australian regimen is 4 g intravenously over 20 minutes followed by 1 g per hour maintenance for 24 hours after delivery. Clinical monitoring (deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate above 12, urine output above 100 mL in 4 hours) replaces routine serum magnesium level measurement. Magnesium is a seizure prophylactic; blood pressure is controlled separately with labetalol, hydralazine or nifedipine.
key_points: AU magnesium sulfate regimen: 4 g intravenous load over 20 minutes then 1 g/h for 24 hours after delivery.
Monitor by clinical signs (reflexes, respiratory rate above 12, urine output above 100 mL/4 h).
Magnesium is a seizure prophylactic, not an antihypertensive; treat blood pressure separately.
explanation.pearls: The Australian magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis regimen is 4 g intravenous load over 20 minutes then 1 g per hour for 24 hours after delivery, monitored by reflexes and respiratory rate rather than by routine serum magnesium levels.

subtopic_detail: Intrapartum penicillin prophylaxis timing and interval for a Group B Streptococcus positive woman in early labour at 39 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 29 year old parous woman at 39 plus 2 weeks in early labour with 4 hours of regular contractions and ruptured membranes 90 minutes ago at home. She is Group B Streptococcus (GBS) positive on a routine 36 week vaginal and rectal swab. She has no penicillin allergy. Her previous baby was well and there was no invasive GBS disease. Cervical examination is 3 cm dilated, cephalic, well applied.

Cardiotocograph shows a normal reactive trace with a baseline of 140 per minute. Temperature is 36.8 degC and she is well. She lives 20 minutes from hospital. The midwife requests advice on intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. Estimated fetal weight is average for gestation and her body mass index is 24 kg per m2. She has no significant comorbidities and no other antibiotic use during the pregnancy or the last 6 months.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 88 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Obstetric: 39+2 weeks, parous, cephalic, 3 cm dilated, membranes ruptured 90 minutes ago
data_table.Microbiology: 36 week vaginal/rectal swab GBS positive; no penicillin allergy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Give a single intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g stat and no further doses for the duration of labour to cover Group B Streptococcus prophylaxis and avoid the need for repeat intravenous antibiotic dosing during labour
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is not the AU first line for GBS prophylaxis in a non allergic woman; benzylpenicillin loading and 4 hourly dosing is standard. (Source: RANZCOG: Group B Streptococcus)

options.text: Withhold intrapartum antibiotics and reassess only if maternal fever develops during labour or if the second stage is delayed beyond 3 hours or membranes rupture greater than 18 hours prior to birth
options.rationale: Culture based GBS colonisation at 36 weeks is itself an indication for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis regardless of clinical risk factors developing. (Source: RANZCOG: Group B Streptococcus)

options.text: Give oral amoxicillin 1 g every 8 hours for the duration of labour with a first dose immediately in the antenatal ward before transfer of care to the birth suite for continuing intrapartum care
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics do not achieve adequate intrapartum foetal blood levels for GBS prophylaxis; the intravenous route is required. (Source: RANZCOG: Group B Streptococcus)

options.text: Give intravenous clindamycin 900 mg every 8 hours for the duration of labour for suspected penicillin allergy with anaphylactic reaction risk despite the woman reporting no penicillin allergy at booking
options.rationale: Clindamycin is second line for anaphylactic penicillin allergy only; a non allergic woman should receive benzylpenicillin. (Source: RANZCOG: Group B Streptococcus)

options.text: Give intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery, aiming for at least one full dose delivered 4 hours or more before delivery to achieve adequate prophylaxis
options.rationale: AU RANZCOG intrapartum GBS prophylaxis in a non allergic woman is intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g every 4 hours; a dose given at least 4 hours before delivery is optimal for neonatal blood levels. (Source: RANZCOG: Group B Streptococcus)

explanation.summary: Group B Streptococcus is the leading cause of early onset neonatal sepsis in Australia. RANZCOG endorses a culture based screening strategy with combined vaginal and rectal swab at 35 to 37 weeks. Positive colonisation, previous baby with invasive GBS disease and GBS bacteriuria in the current pregnancy are indications for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis regardless of other risk factors. Intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g every 4 hours is first line in non allergic women; at least one dose given 4 hours or more before delivery achieves adequate transplacental levels. Cefazolin is used for low risk penicillin allergy and clindamycin (with susceptibility) or vancomycin for high risk allergy. Oral or single dose regimens do not achieve adequate foetal blood levels.
key_points: AU regimen (non allergic): benzylpenicillin 3 g intravenous load then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery.
Aim for at least one full dose 4 hours or more before delivery for adequate foetal blood levels.
Cefazolin for low risk penicillin allergy; clindamycin (with susceptibility) or vancomycin for high risk allergy.
explanation.pearls: Benzylpenicillin 3 g intravenous load then 1.8 g every 4 hours is the AU intrapartum GBS regimen; the dose interval optimisation is the 4 hour rule (at least one dose 4 hours before delivery).
